items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a coherent world view that responds to an issue and is made up of argument, evidence and assumptions, shaped by a particular standpoint”?
items.markingKey: Perspective: a coherent world view that responds to an issue and is made up of argument, evidence and assumptions, shaped by a particular standpoint. [1]

items.stem: Which piece of evidence would give the strongest support to a claim about public opinion on state use of facial recognition surveillance?
options: Whatever the evidence says, the way the world has handled state use of facial recognition surveillance is simply unjust.
A campaign group in Dhaka predicts that, if nothing is done by 2040, this effect will become far more serious: “Misidentification, which studies have found is more common for some ethnic groups”.
“I talked to my neighbours about state use of facial recognition surveillance and they all agreed with me, so I am sure everyone feels the same,” said Lucas, who lives in Madrid.
A survey of 2,500 adults in Valdoria found that 51% think the parliament should ban live facial recognition in public places.
items.answer: A survey of 2,500 adults in Valdoria found that 51% think the parliament should ban live facial recognition in public places.
items.markingKey: A large survey is more representative than an anecdote; a value judgement and a prediction are not evidence of current opinion. [1]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that flaws in reasoning are more common in political debate about the under-representation of women in parliaments than in academic writing about it? Consider different perspectives in your answer.
items.answer: For: Politicians and campaigners aim to persuade quickly, using ad hominem, slippery slope or appeals to popularity. Social media rewards emotional, simplified arguments. Against: Academic writing is peer reviewed, which removes many flaws. Academics can still generalise from small samples or confuse correlation with causation. Judgement: Flaws appear in both, but the purpose and checks of each type of writing affect how common they are.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a person or group with an interest in an issue, who may be affected by it or able to influence it”?
items.markingKey: Stakeholder: a person or group with an interest in an issue, who may be affected by it or able to influence it. [1]

items.stem: A student researching the export of plastic waste to poorer countries needs to decide quickly whether a long report on the issue is relevant. Explain why skimming is a suitable strategy.
items.answer: Skimming saves time and focuses effort: it lets the student decide quickly whether a long report on the issue is relevant without reading every word, so more sources can be considered.
items.markingKey: 1 mark describes the strategy; 1 mark explains why it suits the purpose [1]

items.stem: Argument A: “We should ignore Samuel’s argument that voting should be made compulsory: Samuel dresses badly on television. A democracy works best when governments are chosen by the whole electorate. This is supported by an interview with one family in Dubai. So voting should be made compulsory.” Argument B: “Compulsory voting removes the freedom not to vote. This is supported by a peer-reviewed study comparing 18 countries over ten years. Supporters point out that a democracy works best when governments are chosen by the whole electorate, but this does not outweigh the costs. So it is wrong to say that voting should be made compulsory.” Compare and evaluate the two arguments. Which is more convincing? In your answer consider reasoning, evidence, use of language and the perspectives each represents.
items.answer: Argument B is more convincing: its evidence (a peer-reviewed study comparing 18 countries over ten years) is more reliable and representative, it responds to the opposing view, and it avoids flawed appeals. The other relies on an interview with one family in Dubai and a flawed opening claim. However, both rest on assumptions, e.g. that governments chosen by more of the electorate will be more representative of the electorate’s interests, and more evidence would be needed for a firm judgement.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): describes the arguments with little comparison. Level 2 (3–4 marks): compares the arguments using at least two criteria (evidence, reasoning, language, perspective) with some judgement. Level 3 (5–6 marks): sustained comparison across several criteria, evaluating evidence quality and flaws, leading to a clear, well-supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “presenting someone else’s words or ideas as your own without acknowledgement”?
items.markingKey: Plagiarism: presenting someone else’s words or ideas as your own without acknowledgement. [1]

items.stem: This argument appeared in an opinion column in Bogotá: “In Australia, where voting is compulsory, turnout is usually above 90%. A democracy works best when governments are chosen by the whole electorate. Moreover, compulsory voting forces parties to address the needs of groups that currently stay at home. So compulsory voting would make elected governments more representative. Some people claim that compulsory voting removes the freedom not to vote. However, voters may still spoil their ballot or choose “none of the above”. Therefore, voting should be made compulsory.” What is the function of “So compulsory voting would make elected governments more representative.” in this argument?
items.markingKey: “So compulsory voting would make elected governments more representative.” is the intermediate conclusion. [1]

items.stem: Assess the claim that statistics used in debates about disputes over shared rivers tell us more about the people presenting them than about the issue.
items.answer: For: Statistics are selected and presented to support a perspective (e.g. truncated axes, percentages vs percentage points). Vested interests affect which data are collected and published. Against: Well-collected statistics from neutral sources (statistics offices, peer-reviewed studies) are strong evidence. Misuse can be detected by checking method, sample and presentation. Judgement: Statistics can be strong evidence, but only when their source, method and presentation are evaluated.

Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.markingKey: National perspective: a view of an issue shaped mainly by the interests, culture or policies of one country. [1]

items.stem: A student’s proposed essay question is: “Which international body publishes data on state use of facial recognition surveillance?” What is the main problem with it?
options: It is closed, with a single factual answer
It is descriptive, inviting an account rather than an argument
It focuses on one perspective, so different perspectives cannot be compared
It is too broad to answer in 2,000 words
items.answer: It is closed, with a single factual answer
items.markingKey: It is closed, with a single factual answer. [1]

items.stem: “Threats to press freedom can only be solved through international cooperation.” To what extent do you agree with this statement? You may wish to consider: sovereignty; evidence of what has worked.
items.answer: For: Journalists jailed or killed in many countries, recorded each year by Reporters Without Borders and the Committee to Protect Journalists. Possible international action: protect journalists’ sources and repeal broad “false news” laws (parliament). Against: Much of the problem is national or local: a law that allows a government to shut down news websites accused of “spreading falsehoods”. National or local action such as to raise press freedom in trade and aid agreements can make a difference: external pressure can protect individual journalists. Judgement: International cooperation is necessary for the cross-border dimensions, but most effective responses combine it with national and local action.

items.stem: A speaker says: “Either the riverside governments must ask a neutral mediator such as the African Union or the World Bank to help, or we accept that disputes over shared rivers will never be solved. There is no other choice.” Identify the flaw.
items.markingKey: False dichotomy: presenting only two options when others exist. [1]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that the best way to address corruption in public procurement is for the parliament to create an independent anti-corruption agency with powers to prosecute. You may wish to consider: effectiveness; unintended consequences.
items.answer: For: It can investigate powerful officials without political interference. It acts on a cause of the issue: officials have wide discretion and little oversight when awarding contracts. Against: Agencies can be captured or starved of funds by the politicians they investigate. An alternative is to publish all public contracts online (open contracting): citizens, journalists and rival firms can spot suspicious deals. Judgement: A supported judgement compares actions on effectiveness, feasibility and acceptability, and may recommend a combination.

items.stem: Explain why a student presenting a solution to young people having no say in decisions made by the town council should practise with a timer.
items.answer: It keeps the presentation within the time limit and improves fluency.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that a good conclusion to a Global Perspectives essay should always take a clear side? Consider different perspectives in your answer.
items.answer: For: The question asks for a judgement, so the conclusion must answer it. Sitting on the fence avoids the evaluation the essay has built up. Against: A qualified judgement (it depends on…) can be the most accurate answer. Limitations may mean certainty is not justified. Judgement: A conclusion should give a clear but qualified answer; e.g. on “Should people displaced by climate change be given legal refugee status?”, stating the conditions under which each view holds.
